title: Tatkal 10:00
hook: Tatkal booking opens at 10:00 sharp. 2 lakh people go after 800 seats in the same second, and last time the site was dead by 10:00:01.
context: Railway-style booking site with a burst of demand against a tiny fixed inventory.
solution_brief: Protect the scarce resource: control admission with a waiting room, use short expiring seat holds, randomise within the opening window for fairness, and refund automatically when races still happen. Bottleneck first: hot seat rows and the connection pool. Virtual waiting room to meter demand. Seat holds with TTL, extended once payment starts. Randomised admission plus per-account limits. Automatic compensating refund for late payments.

steps.prompt: At 10:00:01 requests start timing out. Web server CPU is moderate, but database connections are exhausted and many queries are waiting on locks for the same few hundred seat rows. What is failing first?
steps.context_note: 2 lakh requests arrive within a second for 800 seats.

options.text: The web servers, which have run out of CPU capacity to handle the burst
The database: exhausted connections and lock contention on hot rows
The payment gateway, which is rate limiting our calls to it
The CDN, which cannot serve the static assets fast enough

steps.explanation: Queries waiting on locks and an exhausted connection pool point at the database. With 800 seats and 2 lakh requesters, nearly every request contends for the same rows, so work serialises while connections pile up. Web CPU is described as moderate, which rules out the web tier as the first failure.
steps.bottleneck_note: Hot rows serialise writes. More concurrent requests just make the line longer.

steps.prompt: More web servers did not relieve the hot seat rows. What should change at the front of the booking path?
steps.context_note: You tripled the web servers, but the database is still out of connections and the site still falls over.

options.text: Add ten times more web servers so that no single one is overloaded by the spike
Increase the database connection pool to match the larger web tier
Add read replicas for the seat table
Put a virtual waiting room in front that admits users at a controlled rate

steps.explanation: The bottleneck is serialised access to a few rows, so more web servers only send more contenders at them. A waiting room meters demand to what the critical section can take. A bigger connection pool just lets more transactions queue on the same locks, and read replicas do nothing for contended writes.
steps.bottleneck_note: When demand cannot be served, shape it before it reaches the scarce resource.

steps.prompt: A user picks seat 12 and goes to pay. How should the seat be protected during payment without being lost for ever if they abandon?
steps.context_note: Admission is now metered. The next problem is protecting a seat while its buyer pays, which can take minutes.

options.text: Place a hold that expires after a few minutes unless payment completes
Mark the seat as sold immediately and refund the buyer later if payment fails
Hold the seat until the user explicitly cancels or pays
Place no hold, and give the seat to the first payment that succeeds

steps.explanation: A hold with an expiry gives the user a fair window and guarantees the seat returns if they vanish. A hold that needs an explicit cancel leaks seats whenever someone closes the tab, marking seats sold early causes mass refunds, and no hold means people pay for seats they then cannot get.
steps.bottleneck_note: Every temporary claim needs an expiry, or abandoned claims silently eat your inventory.

steps.prompt: Admission is first-come first-served by arrival time. Which change makes it fairer?
steps.context_note: Within one second, arrival order mostly reflects network speed and automation, not effort. Bots are filling the first positions.

options.text: Keep strict first-in first-out, because the order of arrival is already fair to all
Admit the 800 fastest requests straight to booking
Randomise positions in the opening window, one entry per verified account
Admit users in order of account age

steps.explanation: Differences of a few milliseconds measure latency and scripting, not intent. Randomising positions across the opening window removes the advantage of speed, and one entry per verified account blunts multi-tab bots. Account age rewards early sign-ups and shuts out genuine new users.
steps.bottleneck_note: Fairness is a design decision. Strict FIFO rewards the fastest machine, not the person.

steps.prompt: Another user has already bought the seat. How should the system handle this late payment?
steps.context_note: Payment latency varies. This user's payment succeeded at minute 6, after their 5-minute hold expired.

options.text: Give the seat to both users and sort it out on the platform
Refund the late payment automatically and tell the user the seat was taken
Cancel the other user's confirmed ticket and move the late payer into the seat
Keep the payment pending until the user contacts support

steps.explanation: The other user holds a confirmed booking, so the late payer's money must be returned through an automatic compensating refund with a clear message. Extending the hold once payment starts prevents most of these races, but the refund covers the rest. Double-booking or cancelling a confirmed ticket just moves the harm to someone else.
steps.bottleneck_note: Assume timing races will occur and design a compensating action for each one.
